Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan (July/August 644 or June/July 647 - 9 October 705), was the fifth Umayyad caliph, ruling from April 685 until his death in October 705.
Nicknamed the 'Knight King' or 'Soldier King' for his role in World War I, this Belgian monarch succeeded his uncle Leopold II to the throne in 1909 — who was he?
Albert I of Belgium (8 April 1875 - 17 February 1934) was King of the Belgians from 23 December 1909 until his death in 1934.
Born in the colonial Carolinas and married to Rachel Donelson, this Army general turned seventh U.S. president lent his name to a whole democratic movement — who is he?
Andrew Jackson (March 15, 1767 - June 8, 1845) was the seventh president of the United States from 1829 to 1837.
Married to Benazir Bhutto in 1987, this politician later served two separate terms as Pakistan's president, decades apart — who is he?
Asif Ali Zardari (born 26 July 1955) is a Pakistani politician who has served as the 14th president of Pakistan since 2024.
George Washington trusted this major general enough to hand him command of West Point — which he then schemed to surrender to the British in 1780. Who was the would-be turncoat?
Benedict Arnold was British military officer (1741–1801).

Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period

A former Unilever executive who rose to CEO of Air New Zealand, he became leader of the Opposition in 2021 and prime minister two years later — who is he?
Christopher Luxon (born 19 July 1970) is a New Zealand politician and businessman who has served as the 42nd prime minister of New Zealand since 2023.
Nicknamed the 'King of the Wild Frontier,' this American frontiersman represented Tennessee in the U.S. House of Representatives before dying while fighting in the Texas Revolution — who is he?
Davy Crockett (August 17, 1786 - March 6, 1836) was an American politician, militia officer and frontiersman.
Followers of this modern movement pick careers and donate to charities based on rigorous cost-benefit calculations, aiming to maximize positive impact worldwide — what movement is this?
Effective altruism (EA) is a 21st-century philosophical and social movement that advocates impartially calculating benefits and prioritizing causes to provide the greatest good.
This former guerrilla movement, born from a 1980 merger of leftist Salvadoran factions, later became a political party after El Salvador's long civil war ended in 1992 — which group?
Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front is a Salvadoran left-wing political party and former guerrilla rebel group.
Speaking a Continental Celtic language and bearing the hallmarks of La Tène culture, this Iron Age people spread across what is now France, Belgium, and beyond — who were they?
Gauls (Ancient) were a group of Celtic peoples of mainland Europe in the Iron Age and the Roman period (roughly 5th century BC to 5th century AD).

Schooled in exile in the US and Argentina after his party's founder was ousted, he came home to lead the opposition coalition against a military dictatorship — and served as Panama's president from 1989 to 1994. Who was he?
Guillermo Endara (May 12, 1936 - September 28, 2009) was a Panamanian politician who served as the president of Panama from 1989 to 1994.
Cast off Mount Olympus by his mother due to a congenital impairment, this Greek god presided over fire, metalworking, and volcanoes — who is he?
Hephaestus (eight spellings; Ancient) is the Greek god of artisans, blacksmiths, carpenters, craftsmen, fire, metallurgy, metalworking, sculpture, and volcanoes.
Known to the Romans as Somnus, this Greek god of sleep is the namesake behind a word for an induced trance — who is he?
Hypnos (Ancient), also spelled Hypnus, is the personification of sleep.
This criminal-defence lawyer represented Bramalea—Gore—Malton in Ontario's legislature before leading a major Canadian federal party from 2017 to 2025 — who is he?

Jagmeet Singh (born January 2, 1979) is a Canadian politician and lawyer who served as the leader of the New Democratic Party (NDP) from 2017 to 2025 and as the member of Parliament (MP) for Burnaby South from 2019 to 2025.

Having left school at 13 to join Melbourne's labour movement, this Labor leader served as Australia's prime minister through most of WWII's Pacific war and is often ranked among the nation's greatest — who was he?
John Curtin (8 January 1885 - 5 July 1945) was an Australian politician who served as the 14th prime minister of Australia from 1941 until his death in 1945.
This politician represents the Sircilla constituency in the Telangana Legislative Assembly and was named Most Inspirational Icon of 2015 by a major Indian broadcaster — who is he?
K. T. Rama Rao (born 24 July 1976), commonly known as KTR, is an Indian politician and Member of Legislative Assembly (MLA) of Telangana Legislative Assembly.
This American politician served as South Dakota's governor before becoming the eighth U.S. secretary of homeland security in 2025 — who is she?
Kristi Noem (NOHM; ne Arnold; born November 30, 1971) is an American politician serving as the United States special envoy for the Shield of the Americas since 2026.
Before becoming the 28th U.S. secretary of defense, this retired Army general was the first African American to command U.S. Central Command — who is he?
Lloyd Austin (born August 8, 1953) is a retired United States Army general who served as the 28th United States secretary of defense, from 2021 to 2025, under the Biden administration.
Born into the House of Valois in Lorraine, this queen consort of Henry VI became a driving force of the Lancastrian cause in the Wars of the Roses — who is she?
Margaret of Anjou (23 March 1430 - 25 August 1482) was Queen of England by marriage to King Henry VI from 1445 to 1461 and again from 1470 to 1471.
A poet and broadcaster who entered politics through the Labour Party, this Irishman served as mayor of Galway before becoming president of Ireland from 2011 to 2025 — who is he?
Michael D. Higgins (born 18 April 1941) is an Irish politician, poet and broadcaster who served as the president of Ireland from November 2011 to November 2025.

This Indian lawyer and Indian National Congress leader served as party president from 1919 to 1920 and again from 1928 to 1929, and fathered the man who would become independent India's first prime minister — who is he?
Motilal Nehru (6 May 1861 - 6 February 1931) was an Indian lawyer, activist, and politician affiliated with the Indian National Congress.
Before becoming France's president in 2007, this Paris-born politician served as mayor of Neuilly-sur-Seine and led the UMP party — who is it?
Nicolas Sarkozy (sar-KOH-zee; born 28 January 1955) is a French former politician who served as the president of France from 2007 to 2012.

This American showman built fame on celebrated hoaxes and co-founded a legendary circus — though he insisted the cynical phrase 'there's a sucker born every minute' was wrongly pinned on him — who was he?
P. T. Barnum (July 5, 1810 - April 7, 1891) was an American showman, businessman, and politician remembered for promoting celebrated hoaxes and founding the Ringling Bros.
The fifth Roman governor of Judaea under Tiberius, he's named in both the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds — and is even venerated as a saint by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Who is he?
Pontius Pilate was the fifth governor of the Roman province of Judaea, serving under Emperor Tiberius from 26/27 to 36/37 AD.
Nicknamed 'electric brain' for his calm under pressure, this U.S. admiral commanded Task Force 16 at Midway, where American dive bombers sank four Japanese fleet carriers — who was he?
Raymond A. Spruance (July 3, 1886 - December 13, 1969) was a United States Navy admiral during World War II.

Sparked in 1917 amid wartime bread shortages and battlefield defeats, this upheaval abolished a monarchy and installed a socialist government after two successive uprisings and a civil war — what is it called?
Russian Revolution was a period of political and social change in Russia, starting in 1917.
This liberal, pro-European Ukrainian party takes its name from a sitcom starring the man who'd go on to become the country's real president — which party?
Servant of the People (SN) is a liberal, centrist, pro-European political party in Ukraine.
This ruler quelled a rebellion in Gdańsk and worked closely with chancellor Jan Zamoyski during his decade as king of Poland — who was he?

Stephen Báthory (27 September 1533 - 12 December 1586) was King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania as well as Prince of Transylvania (1576-1586), after previously being Voivode of Transylvania (1571-1576).
This German politician has co-chaired the far-right Alternative for Germany party since 2019 alongside Alice Weidel, and is known for pro-Russian, eurosceptic foreign-policy views. Who is he?
Tino Chrupalla (born 14 April 1975) is a German politician from the far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD).
After heading the Soviet gas ministry, this man became Gazprom's first chairman, then Russia's Prime Minister for six years during the transition from a planned to a market economy — who is he?
Viktor Chernomyrdin (9 April 1938 - 3 November 2010) was a Soviet and Russian politician and businessman.
Praised for strategy but condemned for scorched-earth tactics against the Confederacy, this Ohio-born Union general from a politically prominent family graduated West Point in 1840 — who was he?
William Tecumseh Sherman (tih-; February 8, 1820 - February 14, 1891) was an American businessman, author, and United States Army general in the Union Army during the American Civil War (1861-1865).

After 30 years without one, France got a woman back in its top government post in May 2022—the second ever to hold it. A civil engineer and transport minister, who took the reins during a time of national transition?

Élisabeth Borne (born 18 April 1961) is a French politician who served as Prime Minister of France from May 2022 to January 2024, becoming the second woman to hold the position of Prime Minister and the first in 30 years.
This Austrian-born politician became chancellor of Germany in 1933 and took the title Führer the next year, launching the Second World War with his 1939 invasion of Poland — who was he?
Adolf Hitler: Dictator of Germany from 1933 to 1945.
A five-term Italian prime minister and Christian Democracy leader, this statesman was kidnapped by the far-left Red Brigades in March 1978 — who was he?
Aldo Moro: Prime Minister of Italy (1963–1968; 1974–1976)

American Indian Wars: Frontier conflicts in North America, 1609–1890s.

Anthony Eden: UK Prime Minister from 1955 to 1957.

Atal Bihari Vajpayee: Prime Minister of India (1996; 1998–99, 1999–2004)

Fought on July 4, 1187, between Crusader states and Saladin's Ayyubid forces, this battle removed the Crusaders' capability to wage war in the Holy Land and returned military dominance to the Muslims. It's named for a nearby extinct volcano. What is it?
Battle of Hattin: 1187 Saladin victory over the Crusaders.
This American professor co-founded the far-left Weather Underground in 1969, a group that bombed public buildings against the Vietnam War and was branded domestic terrorists by the FBI — who is he?
Bill Ayers: American professor and activist. William Charles Ayers (born December 26, 1944) is an American retired professor and former community organizer.
The only known biological son of Julius Caesar, this last pharaoh of Ancient Egypt co-ruled with his mother Cleopatra VII before his execution by Octavian — who was he?
Caesarion: Pharaoh of Egypt from 44 to 30 BC.

Founded in 1910 in Paris by its trailblazing namesake, this house ditched corseted silhouettes for functional garments and is famous for its No. 5 perfume and signature Suit — which luxury fashion house?
Chanel: French fashion house. Chanel ( shə-NEL, French: [ʃanɛl]) is a French luxury fashion house founded in 1910 by Coco Chanel in Paris.
Killed alongside Benito Mussolini by Italian partisans in April 1945, this woman was the Italian dictator's mistress — who was she?

Clara Petacci: Mistress of the Italian dictator Benito Mussolini (1912–1945). Clara "Claretta" Petacci (Italian: [klaˈretta peˈtattʃi]; 28 February 1912 – 28 April 1945) was a mistress of the Italian dictator Benito Mussolini.

A former financial analyst for Merrill Lynch subsidiaries, this Taiwanese politician became a Legislative Yuan member in 2022 and ran as Ko Wen-je's vice-presidential running mate in the 2024 Taiwanese presidential election — who is she?
Cynthia Wu: Taiwanese business executive and politician.

Believed to cause possession requiring an exorcism, this class of malevolent supernatural being has roots stretching back to the Paleolithic age and entered Jewish tradition via Zoroastrian influence during the Persian era — what is it?
Demon: Evil supernatural being. The original Ancient Greek word daimōn (δαίμων) did not carry negative connotations, as it denotes a spirit or divine power.

Before leading the commission that investigated the 1963 Kennedy assassination, which California governor became chief justice and authored the majority opinions in Brown v. Board of Education and Miranda v. Arizona?

Euroscepticism: Body of criticism of the European Union.

Five Star Movement: Italian political party. The Five Star Movement (Italian: Movimento 5 Stelle [moviˈmento ˈtʃiŋkwe ˈstelle], M5S) is a political party in Italy, led by Giuseppe Conte.
The first female student at Abeokuta Grammar School, this Nigerian educator and women's-rights organizer wove together anti-imperialist, Pan-Africanist, and feminist ideals — who is she?
The eldest son of former Indonesian president Joko Widodo, this politician became vice president in 2024 as running mate to Prabowo Subianto after serving as mayor of Surakarta — who is he?
Gibran Rakabuming Raka: Vice President of Indonesia since 2024.
Colombia's first left-wing president, he joined a guerrilla movement at just 17 before later founding a party called the Historic Pact — who is he?
Gustavo Petro: President of Colombia since 2022.
He was Iran's top negotiator with the EU three before becoming the country's seventh president in 2013 — which sharia-lawyer-turned-cleric served until 2021?
Hassan Rouhani: President of Iran from 2013 to 2021. Hassan Rouhani (born Hassan Fereydoun, 12 November 1948) is an Iranian politician who served as the seventh president of Iran from 2013 to 2021.

A former first lady, New York senator, and secretary of state, she became the first woman to win a major U.S. party's presidential nomination and the only one to win the popular vote for president — who is she?
Hillary Clinton: American politician and diplomat (born 1947)
Born in Glasgow to Pakistani immigrants, this politician rose from health secretary to lead the SNP and serve as First Minister of Scotland from 2023 to 2024 — who is he?
Humza Yousaf: First Minister of Scotland from 2023 to 2024. Following Ahmad's death in 2009, Yousaf went on to work as a parliamentary assistant for both Alex Salmond and Sturgeon.
Established in 1922 under a treaty that ended a war of independence against British rule, this dominion comprised 26 of 32 counties while the remaining six opted out — what was it called?
Irish Free State: British dominion in Europe from 1922 to 1937.
The only sitting member of the U.S. House ever elected president, this 20th commander-in-chief died in 1881 after being shot just months into office — who is he?
James A. Garfield: President of the United States in 1881.
Founded in 1540 by Ignatius of Loyola and six companions with Pope Paul III's blessing, this Rome-based order is the largest Catholic male religious order and a powerhouse in education — what is it?
Jesuits: Male religious congregation of the Catholic Church.
Born in 1995, he became the youngest president of France's National Rally in 2022, having served as its spokesman and an MEP since 2019 — which French politician is it?
Jordan Bardella: French politician (born 1995). Before becoming acting president of the RN, Bardella served as vice-president from 2019 to 2021 and the party's spokesman from 2017 to 2019.
Dubbed the 'Kingmaker' of 1960s Indian politics for elevating two future prime ministers to power, this former Chief Minister of Madras dropped out of school early — who was he?

Established as a federal holiday in 1894 and celebrated on the first Monday of September, this U.S. observance honors the contributions of American workers — which holiday?
Labor Day: Federal holiday in the United States.
Built on individual rights, consent of the governed, private property and equality before the law, this philosophy is often called the dominant ideology of modern history — what is it?
Liberalism: Philosophy of individual rights and liberty. Liberalism became a distinct movement in the Age of Enlightenment, gaining popularity among Western philosophers and economists.

A major theorist of the Négritude cultural movement, this poet-politician became independent Senegal's first president in 1960 after advocating for African rights within a French federal structure - who is he?
Léopold Sédar Senghor: First president of Senegal, poet, and cultural theorist (1906–2001)

He served the final weeks as president of the Commonwealth, then became the very first president of an independent Philippine republic once the U.S. ceded sovereignty in 1946 — only to die in office two years later. Who was he?
Manuel Roxas: President of the Philippines from 1946 to 1948.
Awarded the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize, this Venezuelan opposition leader founded a vote-monitoring group and later presented her medal to the U.S. president following Maduro's capture — who is she?

Mohammad Reza Pahlavi: Shah of Iran from 1941 to 1979.
Son of a former prime minister, this Malaysian led his country from 2009 until corruption charges involving his family handed his coalition an unprecedented 2018 defeat — who is he?

Operation Praying Mantis: 1988 US attack on Iran in the Iran-Iraq War.
This senior Soviet intelligence officer orchestrated Leon Trotsky's assassination in Mexico in 1940 and later ran spy operations targeting the Manhattan Project — who was he?
The fifth governor of Roman Judaea under Tiberius, he presided over the trial of Jesus — and is so central to Christianity that he's named in both the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds; who is he?
Pontius Pilate: Roman governor of Judea and condemner of Jesus.

Republic of Texas: Country in North America (1836–1846)

Septimius Severus: Roman emperor from 193 to 211. Lucius Septimius Severus (Latin: [ˈluːkius sepˈtimius seˈweːrus]; 11 April 145 – 4 February 211) was Roman emperor from 193 to 211.
Fought in two stages, a winter and summer campaign from 1614 to 1615, this conflict ended the Toyotomi clan and cemented Tokugawa rule over Japan — which historic clash?
Siege of Osaka: 1614-15 series of battles in Japan at the end of the Sengoku Period.

This doctrine holding that governing authority is legitimate to some degree — especially over taxation and production — gained traction in American political discourse during the 1930s and '40s, its opposite being anarchism — what's it called?

Statism: Doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree. In political science, statism or etatism (from French, état 'state') is the doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree.

The first Asian to lead the United Nations, this Burmese diplomat served a record ten years and one month as Secretary-General starting in 1961 — who was he?
U Thant: UN Secretary-General from 1961 to 1971.

Raiding, trading, and settling from Scandinavia across Europe, North Africa, and even Newfoundland between the late 8th and 11th centuries, this seafaring people helped establish Kievan Rus'. Who were they?
Vikings: Norse seafarers, merchants and raiders.
Launched by the United States after the September 11 attacks, this global campaign targeted al-Qaeda, the Taliban, and later Iraq's Ba'athist regime — what was it called?
War on terror: Military campaign following the September 11 attacks.
First achieved in Australasia before spreading to Europe and the Americas, this democratic right for female voters began its 'first wave' in 1893 in English-speaking countries — what right?
Women's suffrage: Legal right of women to vote.
Revered as the Father of the Nation, this ruler of Abu Dhabi became the first president of a newly unified Gulf federation in 1971?
Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan: President of the United Arab Emirates from 1971 to 2004.

Jack Parsons is a chemist. John Whiteside Parsons (born Marvel Whiteside Parsons; October 2, 1914 – June 17, 1952) was an American rocket engineer, chemist, and Thelemite occultist.
What is the atomic number of Mendelevium?
Mendelevium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Md (formerly Mv) and atomic number 101.
In what year was Stephen Hawking born?
Stephen Hawking: Hawking was born in Oxford into a family of physicians.
In what year did Isaac Newton die?
Isaac Newton: Newton contributed to and refined the scientific method, and his work is considered the most influential in bringing forth modern science.
In what year was Potassium discovered?
Potassium is a chemical element; it has symbol K (from Neo-Latin kalium) and atomic number 19.
SEPECAT Jaguar: Breguet Aviation. As of 2026, the Jaguar remains in service with only the Indian Air Force.
Which country is Curtiss P-40 Warhawk from?
Curtiss P-40 Warhawk: United States. The Curtiss P-40 Warhawk is an American single-engined, single-seat, all-metal fighter-bomber that first flew in 1938.
Who is credited with discovering Palladium?
Palladium: William Hyde Wollaston. Palladium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Pd and atomic number 46.
Who is credited with discovering Pectin?
Pectin: Henri Braconnot. The principal chemical component of pectin is galacturonic acid (a sugar acid derived from galactose).
Who is credited with discovering Oxygen?
Oxygen: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Oxygen is a chemical element; it has the symbol O and its atomic number is 8.
The simplest alkyne, this colorless gas owes its straight-line shape to a carbon-carbon triple bond — and though pure it's odorless, commercial grades reek thanks to impurities. What is it?
Acetylene (systematic name: ethyne) is a chemical compound with the formula C2H2 and structure HCCH.
This Indian economist won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for his work on welfare economics and has also studied the causes of famines — who is he?
Amartya Sen (born 3 November 1933) is an Indian economist and philosopher.
Found only on male deer, except reindeer, this branching structure of bone and cartilage falls off and regrows from scratch each year — what is it?
Antler are extensions of an animal's skull found in members of the Cervidae (deer) family.
Caused by poor circulation, lost nerve supply, or simple disuse, this process shrinks a cell, organ, or tissue below its normal mature size — what's it called?
Atrophy is the partial or complete wasting away of a part of the body.

Known only from larval and juvenile specimens until video footage of much larger adults surfaced, this deep-sea cephalopod genus holds its long, elbow-like arms perpendicular to its body — what is it?
Bigfin squid are a group of rarely seen cephalopods with a distinctive morphology.
This flowering plant family is known for flowers with four petals arranged in a cross shape, and includes crops ranging from leafy greens to root vegetables to condiment seeds. Name the family?
Brassicaceae (the older but equally valid) Cruciferae is a medium-sized and economically important family of flowering plants commonly known as the mustards, the crucifers, or the cabbage family.

Spread through contact with infected feces and capable of killing up to 91% of untreated cases, this highly contagious virus mainly strikes dogs and wolves but can also infect foxes, cats, and skunks — what's the virus?
Canine parvovirus (also referred to as CPV, CPV2, or parvo) is a contagious virus mainly affecting dogs and wolves.

The only living member of its genus, this big cat sprints at up to 104 km/h thanks to powerful hindlimbs, long legs, and a flexible spine, and wears black tear-like streaks down its face; which animal is it?
Cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) is a species of large feline and the only living member of the genus Acinonyx.

Native to western South America, this shrub bears oval leaves and red berries, and when its leaves are chewed or brewed as tea they act as a mild stimulant with no evidence of addiction — which plant is it?
Coca refers to any of the four cultivated plants in the family Erythroxylaceae, native to western South America.
Native to North America and smaller than its close relative the gray wolf, this canine fills a similar ecological niche to the golden jackal of Eurasia — which animal?
Coyote (Canis latrans) is a species of canine also known as the American jackal, prairie wolf, and brush wolf.
Defined as having at least three loose or watery bowel movements in a day, this common condition can quickly cause dehydration, especially in children. What condition is it?
Diarrhea (American English), also spelled diarrhoea (British English), is the condition of having at least three loose, liquid, or watery bowel movements in a day.
This English physician created the world's first vaccine, targeting smallpox, and in doing so coined the very term 'vaccine' — derived from the Latin for 'pustules of the cow.' Who was he?
Edward Jenner (17 May 1749 - 26 January 1823) was an English physician and scientist who pioneered the concept of vaccines and created the smallpox vaccine, the world's first vaccine.
The major female sex hormone, this estrogen steroid drives the development of breasts and a female pattern of fat distribution and regulates the menstrual cycle — which one is it?
Estradiol (E2), also called oestrogen, oestradiol, is an estrogen steroid hormone and the major female sex hormone.

Sometimes mistakenly called a cat despite belonging to the weasel family, this North American forest-dwelling carnivore is the only living species in its genus and is larger than the martens it resembles — what animal is it?
Fisher (animal) (Pekania pennanti) is a carnivorous mammal native to North America, a forest-dwelling creature whose range covers much of the boreal forest in Canada to the northern United States.

The first person in Germany to hold a professorship dedicated to experimental physics, he is remembered for his posthumous 'waste book' notebooks and for the tree-like electrical discharge patterns named after him. Who is he?
Georg Christoph Lichtenberg (1 July 1742 - 24 February 1799) was a German physicist, satirist, and Anglophile.
This branch of medicine focuses on the female reproductive system, and when combined with the study of pregnancy and childbirth forms the field known as OB-GYN — name the specialty?
Gynaecology (or gynecology in American English) is the area of medicine concerned with conditions affecting the female reproductive system.

First described by an English physician in 1832, this cancer of the lymphocytes is identified by giant multinucleated Reed-Sternberg cells in the lymph nodes, and about half its cases trace back to the Epstein-Barr virus. What is it?
Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) is a cancer where multinucleated Reed-Sternberg cells (RS cells) are present in the lymph nodes.

Forming at or below zero degrees Celsius, this naturally occurring crystalline solid is technically classified as a mineral and appears on Earth, other planets, and even in interstellar space — what is it?
Ice is water that is frozen into a solid state, typically forming at or below temperatures of 0 C, 32 F, or 273.15 K.
Trained in biochemistry and physiology before ranging into geography and anthropology, this American author won the 1998 Pulitzer for Guns, Germs, and Steel — who is he?
Jared Diamond (born September 10, 1937) is an American scientist, historian, and author.

This childhood illness of unknown cause mainly affects kids under five, causing a prolonged fever lasting more than five days that doesn't respond to typical fever-reducing medicine, plus inflamed blood vessels throughout the body — name the syndrome?
Kawasaki disease (also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome) is a syndrome of unknown cause that results in a fever and mainly affects children under 5 years of age.
With about 180,000 described species — roughly 10% of all known living organisms — which insect order is the second largest, trailing only the beetles?
Lepidoptera are an order of winged insects which include butterflies and moths.
Serving under Chancellor Adenauer, this economist championed West Germany's postwar economic miracle before becoming chancellor himself in 1963 — who is he?
Ludwig Erhard (4 February 1897 - 5 May 1977) was a German politician and economist who served as the second chancellor of West Germany from 1963 until 1966.
The heaviest and largest members of the squirrel family, these 15 species of grazing ground-dwellers vanish each winter to hibernate underground — what are they?
Marmot are large ground squirrels in the genus Marmota, with 15 species living in Asia, Europe, and North America.

An advanced modification of the Korean War-era MiG-15, this Soviet transonic fighter jet entered production in 1952, was license-built in both China and Poland, and remains in North Korean service today — what's the aircraft?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-17 (NATO reporting name: Fresco) is a transonic fighter aircraft that was produced in the Soviet Union from 1952 and was operated by air forces internationally.
Lacking a cell wall entirely, this tiny bacterial species causes a form of atypical lung infection linked to cold agglutinin disease — which microbe first isolated as the 1944 'Eaton agent'?
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a species of very small-cell bacteria that lack a cell wall, in the class Mollicutes.
Sold in packs needing a desiccant to keep it from absorbing moisture, this seaweed sheet was once used as currency and shrine offerings in Japan — what is it?
Nori is a dried edible seaweed used in Japanese cuisine, usually made from species of the red algae genus Pyropia, including P. yezoensis and P. tenera.
Part of the Bovidae family, this genus of seven social species is better known simply as sheep, all thought to trace back to the wild mouflon — which genus?
Ovis is a genus of mammals, part of the Caprinae subfamily of the ruminant family Bovidae.

Which American chemist was the first to synthesize physostigmine and pioneered making progesterone and testosterone from plant sterols — even starting a company to extract steroid intermediates from wild Mexican yams?
Percy Lavon Julian (April 11, 1899 - April 19, 1975) was an American research chemist and a pioneer in the chemical synthesis of medicinal drugs from plants.
This zodiac sign's Latin name means 'fishes,' and it's where the ecliptic crosses the celestial equator near the March equinox — which one?
Pisces (constellation) is a constellation of the zodiac. It is between Aquarius, of similar size, to the southwest and Aries, which is smaller, to the east.

Caused by a mutation in a single gene that holds the cell nucleus together, this rare disorder makes children age much faster than normal, with most patients living only into their teens or twenties — what's the condition?
Progeria (also Hutchinson-Gilford syndrome or Hutchinson-Gilford progeroid syndrome; HGPS) is a type of progeroid syndrome.

Cultivated mainly for its oil-rich seeds, this yellow-flowered Brassica crop is the source of a low-toxicity oil marketed under a Canadian-coined name, and ranks as the world's third-largest vegetable oil source — what is it?
Operating under a pseudonym borrowed from The Princess Bride, this American created the first modern darknet marketplace before his 2013 FBI arrest — who is he?
Ross Ulbricht (born March 27, 1984) is an American cybercriminal who created and operated Silk Road, the first modern darknet market, from 2011 until his arrest in 2013.
Most episodes of this brain-activity disruption last under two minutes and leave the person confused or fatigued afterward, but one lasting over five minutes is a medical emergency — what is it?
Seizure is a sudden disruption of brain activity caused by excessive, synchronized neuronal firing that results in changes in behavior.
With the formula Na2CO3, this odorless white salt yields an alkaline solution in water and earned the name 'soda ash' because plant ashes once gave it up. What is it?
Sodium carbonate (also known as washing soda, soda ash, sal soda, and soda crystals) is the inorganic compound with the formula Na2CO3 and its various hydrates.

Harvested from the seeds of the nux-vomica tree, this bitter colorless alkaloid is infamous as a poison for rodents and birds — yet was once doled out in tiny doses to stimulate the heart and bowels. What is it?
Strychnine (-nin, US chiefly -nyne) is a highly toxic, colorless, bitter, crystalline alkaloid used as a pesticide, particularly for killing small vertebrates such as birds and rodents.
A colorless, water-miscible cyclic ether and a versatile solvent, this compound is mainly used as a precursor to polymers and is an isomer of butanone — what is it?
Tetrahydrofuran (THF), or oxolane, is an organic compound with the formula (CH2)4O.

A phenylpiperazine compound in the serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor class, this antidepressant treats depression, anxiety and insomnia but carries a rare risk of prolonged, painful erections — which drug?
Trazodone is an antidepressant medication used to treat major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, and insomnia.
Once classified in the honeysuckle family before molecular studies gave it its own, this genus of 150-plus shrub species reaches Africa only via the Atlas Mountains — which genus?
Viburnum is a genus of about 150-175 species of flowering plants in the family Viburnaceae.

This Greek economist served as Finance Minister under PM Alexis Tsipras during the 2015 debt crisis, becoming internationally known for opposing EU-imposed austerity, before co-founding the left-wing party DiEM25 — who is he?
Yanis Varoufakis (born 24 March 1961) is a Greek economist, academic, author, and politician.

Nicknamed wolfsbane, monkshood, and devil's helmet, this highly toxic genus of over 250 mountain-dwelling flowering plants thrives in moist, well-draining soils across the Northern Hemisphere — what is it?
Aconitum: Genus of flowering plants in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae.
Which Swiss chemist was the first person to synthesize and personally experience the effects of LSD, later isolating the active compounds in magic mushrooms?
Native to North America but now invasive across Europe after being introduced, this semiaquatic mustelid preys on rodents, fish, and frogs — which animal?
American mink: Semiaquatic species of mustelid. Because of range expansion, the American mink is classed as a least-concern species by the IUCN.
Belonging to the suborder Vermilingua and closely related to sloths, these mammals include giant, silky, and tamandua species that feed almost exclusively on ants and termites — what are they called?
Anteater: Mammals known for eating ants and termites.
Native to eastern North America's wet woods and swamps, this shrub genus produces bitter 'chokeberries' that reached Scandinavia and Russia by the eighteenth century — what genus is this?

Aronia: Genus of plants (chokeberries). Aronia is a genus of deciduous shrubs, the chokeberries, in the family Rosaceae native to eastern North America and most commonly found in wet woods and swamps.
This Mexican mole salamander never grows up — it reaches sexual maturity while staying fully aquatic with feathery external gills, skipping metamorphosis entirely. What is it?
Axolotl: Species of salamander. The axolotl (from Classical Nahuatl: āxōlōtl [aːˈʃoːloːtɬ]; Ambystoma mexicanum) is a species of mole salamander.
Named after the aromatic resin from which it was first derived, this simplest aromatic carboxylic compound forms salts widely used as food preservatives — what is it called?

Native to North America and classified in the genus Vaccinium, this fruit comes in wild 'lowbush' and cultivated 'highbush' varieties, with Canada leading global production of the wild type — what fruit is it?
Blueberry: Perennial plant with blue berries.
Known for a widely viewed 2010 TEDx talk on shame and vulnerability, which academic wrote six consecutive number-one New York Times bestsellers, including Daring Greatly?
Brené Brown: American academic, speaker and author.
Found in chalk, limestone, eggshells, and pearls alike, this CaCO3 compound is also the active ingredient in agricultural lime and doubles as an antacid — what is it?
Calcium carbonate: Chemical compound. Materials containing much calcium carbonate or resembling it are described as calcareous.

Discovered as a single well-preserved skeleton in Argentina's Chubut Province in 1984, this short-snouted, lightly built predator belongs to a South American branch of large theropods — which dinosaur genus?
Carnotaurus: Genus of dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous period.
With independently swiveling eyes, a projectile tongue, and the ability to shift colors, this Old World lizard family is famous for camouflage — which reptile?
Chameleon: Family of reptiles. The members of this family are best known for their distinct range of colours, being capable of colour-shifting camouflage.
This fluoroquinolone antibiotic treats everything from typhoid fever to urinary tract infections but can rarely cause tendon rupture — what drug?
Ciprofloxacin: Fluoroquinolone antibiotic. Ciprofloxacin, sold under the brand name Cipro among others, is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic used to treat a number of bacterial infections.

Nicknamed 'flying lemurs' despite not being lemurs at all, these Southeast Asian gliding mammals are primates' closest living relatives and belong to an order whose name means 'skin wing' — what are they called?
Going by puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther depending on where you stand, this big cat is the most widely distributed wild land mammal in the Americas — what is it?
Cougar: Wild cat species native to the Americas.
Native to Mexico and Central America, this tuberous flowering plant blooms in nearly every hue except blue, and its tubers store energy as inulin rather than starch — what is it?
Dahlia: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.
Approved for medical use in the US back in 1950, this medication treats intestinal spasms such as those seen in irritable bowel syndrome — what is it called?
Nicknamed 'Viking disease,' this hand condition — first surgically treated in 1831 by the surgeon it's named after — permanently curls the ring finger inward. What is it?
Dupuytren's contracture: Medical condition featuring permanent bending of fingers.
A Swedish scientist and inventor until, at 53, dreams and visions sent him into a spiritual phase, this polymath became best known for his 1758 book on the afterlife, Heaven and Hell — who was he?
Emanuel Swedenborg: Swedish scientist, philosopher, and theologian (1688–1772)
With a sweet smell like pear drops, this colorless solvent turns up in nail-polish remover and is used to decaffeinate tea and coffee. What is it?
Named after a 19th-century English physicist, this SI unit measures a material's ability to store electrical charge, equal to one coulomb per volt — what is it?
Farad: SI unit of electric capacitance.
Patented in 1962 and sold under a brand name synonymous with 'roofies,' this benzodiazepine is notoriously linked to date-rape drug use — what is it?
Flunitrazepam: Benzodiazepine sedative. Flunitrazepam, sold under the brand name Rohypnol among others, is a benzodiazepine used to treat severe insomnia and assist with anesthesia.
Born in Pisa in 1564, this Italian polymath has been crowned the father of observational astronomy and the scientific method — and was among the earliest tinkerers to build a thermoscope. Who is he?
Galileo Galilei: Italian physicist and astronomer (1564–1642)

This Italian friar and cosmological theorist proposed that stars were distant suns with their own planets, and was tried for heresy by the Roman Inquisition for insisting the universe is infinite — who was he?
Giordano Bruno: Italian Dominican friar, philosopher and mathematician (1548–1600)
This junctional area between the torso and thigh, where the lower abdominal wall meets the leg, is commonly strained in a familiar sports injury — what is it called?
Groin: Area between the torso and the thigh. In human anatomy, the groin, also known as the inguinal region or iliac region, is the junctional area between the torso and the thigh.
This wingless insect spends its entire life on the human scalp, sipping blood, and can neither fly nor jump — its short stumpy legs can't even walk well on a flat surface. What tiny freeloader is it?
Head louse: Insect parasite of humans.
Also called urticaria, this skin condition brings red or flesh-colored raised, itchy bumps that may sting and often follow an allergic reaction — what is it?
Hives: Skin disease characterized by red, raised, and itchy bumps.
Named from Greek words meaning "over" and "formation," this condition enlarges tissue by increasing the number of cells rather than their size — which term, distinct from hypertrophy?
Hyperplasia: Enlargement of tissue due to cell proliferation.
This sugar alcohol, with about half the sweetness of table sugar, is made by the human kidney at roughly two grams a day and reaches its highest concentration in the brain — what is it?
Inositol: Carbocyclic sugar. Its formula is C6H12O6; the molecule has a ring of six carbon atoms, each with a hydrogen atom and a hydroxy group (–OH).
This fragrant genus of shrubs and vines in the olive family is grown in vast quantities in one Egyptian village that supplies much of the world's perfume industry — which plant?
Jasmine: Genus of flowering plant in the olive family Oleaceae.
Born Giulia Maddalena Angela in Italy, this physician became a leading freethinker and activist for women's rights and social reform in early-20th-century Argentina — who is she?
Julieta Lanteri: Argentine doctor and activist (1873–1932)
Biosynthesized in the body from the amino acid tyrosine, this compound is the direct precursor to dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine — what is it?
L-DOPA: Chemical compound. As is true for many molecules, the human body produces only one of these isomers (the l-DOPA form).

Elon Musk's praise for his MIT driver-attention study on Tesla's autopilot brought this computer scientist to prominence in 2019, ahead of a career hosting long-form interviews with notable figures — who is he?
Lex Fridman: American scientist and podcast host (born 1983)
Sold under the brand name Cozaar, this angiotensin receptor blocker treats high blood pressure while also protecting the kidneys in diabetic patients — what drug is it?
Losartan: Blood pressure medication. Losartan, sold under the brand name Cozaar among others, is a medication used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension).
Known by the common English name 'mallow,' this plant genus bears palmately lobed leaves and five-petaled flowers ranging from pink to white — which genus?

Marked by small white Koplik spots inside the mouth and a red rash that starts on the face before spreading, this highly contagious, vaccine-preventable disease can bring fevers over 40°C — which disease?
This theoretical physicist and science communicator bridged science and science fiction well enough to win a 2021 lifetime achievement award named for Arthur C. Clarke — who is he?
Michio Kaku: American theoretical physicist, futurist and author.

Thought to enjoy 'hybrid vigor' and a reduced risk of inbreeding-linked health problems, this catch-all term covers roughly 150 million dogs worldwide that don't belong to any officially recognized breed — what's it called?
Named for its resemblance to a tiny mouse's ear, this flowering plant genus is known in the Northern Hemisphere by a romantic common name and is Alaska's official flower — what is it?
Myosotis: Genus of flowering plants in the family Boraginaceae.
This synthetic element 113 was claimed by both a Russian-American team at Dubna and, in 2004, a Japanese team at Riken. What's its name?
Nihonium: Chemical element with atomic number 113 (Nh)

Distinct from an unrelated American family with a similar name, these small seed-eating birds include house- and tree-dwelling species that nest on buildings in huge city numbers — which bird family is this?
Old World sparrow: Family of songbirds. Old World sparrows are groups of small passerine birds forming the family Passeridae.
Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1993, this scripting language's name began as 'Personal Home Page' before becoming a recursive backronym meaning 'Hypertext Preprocessor' — what is it?
PHP: Scripting language created in 1994. PHP is a general-purpose scripting language geared towards web development.
Derived from Greek words meaning 'healer of children,' this branch of medicine covers care from infancy through adolescence — what is it?
Pediatrics: Branch of medicine caring for children. Within the Commonwealth, pediatrics covers patients until the age of 18, except in India where the pediatric age is 12.
Formed by stripping three protons from phosphoric acid, this triply-charged ion carries the formula PO4³⁻ and lends its name to esters like trimethyl ester in organic chemistry — what anion is it?
Phosphate: Anion, salt, functional group or ester derived from a phosphoric acid.
Named after a French mathematician and physicist, this materials-science measure captures how much a material bulges sideways when compressed lengthwise — what is it?
Poisson's ratio: Measure of material deformation perpendicular to loading.

Diagnosed in about 8% of male urology visits in the US, this umbrella term covers several bacterial and non-bacterial pelvic conditions, despite its name not always involving actual inflammation — which condition?
Prostatitis: Medical condition. Prostatitis is an umbrella term for a variety of medical conditions that incorporate bacterial and non-bacterial origin illnesses in the pelvic region.
Named partly for Jack Northrop, designer of a tailless aircraft, which genus of enormous azhdarchid pterosaur is a top candidate for the largest flying animal ever?
Quetzalcoatlus: Genus of azhdarchid pterosaurs from the Late Cretaceous.

Marked by tea-colored urine and triggered by crush injuries or extreme exertion, this condition involves skeletal muscle breaking down so fast that released myoglobin can damage the kidneys — what is it called?
Rhabdomyolysis: Condition in which damaged skeletal muscle breaks down rapidly.
What term describes herbivorous mammals like cattle and giraffes that digest plant matter by regurgitating and re-chewing it as cud?
Ruminant: Hoofed herbivorous grazing or browsing mammals.
Driven by an empirical cycle of observation, hypothesis, testing, and conclusion, this systematic discipline splits into natural and social branches. What is it?
Science: Systematic endeavour to gain knowledge.
Also called herpes zoster, this viral disease paints a painful blistering rash down just one side of the body, and can leave lingering nerve pain called postherpetic neuralgia — what is it?
Shingles: Viral disease caused by the varicella zoster virus.

Known as sun spiders, camel spiders, or wind scorpions, this arachnid order is neither true spider nor scorpion, and urban legends wildly exaggerate its size, speed, and danger to humans — what is it?
Solifugae: Order of arachnids. The order includes more than 1,000 described species in about 147 genera.
Fired by Apple's board in 1985, he founded NeXT and bought a animation studio before returning a decade later to revolutionize consumer tech. Who?
Steve Jobs: American businessman and inventor (1955–2011)
Serving as prime minister of Turkey seven separate times before becoming president from 1993 to 2000, he was also the first PM to have been born in the Turkish Republic — who was he?

Süleyman Demirel: President of Turkey from 1993 to 2000. Demirel was the leader of the opposition from 1971 to 1975 before forming a right-wing government known as the First Nationalist Front, which collapsed in 1977.
With more than 8,000 species known for their loud mating calls and leaf-like camouflage, this insect family also goes by the common name katydids or bush crickets — which family?
Tettigoniidae: Family of insects. Insects in the family Tettigoniidae are commonly called katydids (especially in North America) or bush crickets.
This colorless solvent's sweet smell partly explains the aroma of gasoline and paint fumes, and its IUPAC name is simply methylbenzene — which aromatic hydrocarbon is it?
Toluene: Aromatic hydrocarbon. Toluene is a colorless, water-insoluble liquid with a sweet smell, and is partially responsible for the aroma of gasoline and paint fumes.
First flown in 1952, this nuclear-capable Soviet bomber is the only turboprop strategic bomber still flying — its contra-rotating propellers earning it the NATO nickname 'Bear.' What is it?
Tupolev Tu-95: Russian strategic bomber aircraft.
This hairy biennial plant can top two meters, packing small yellow flowers onto a tall spike that sprouts from a low leaf rosette in disturbed, sunlit soil — which weedy species?
Verbascum thapsus: Species of plant. It is a hairy biennial plant that can grow to 2 m tall or more.

Distinguished by its wide, square-lipped mouth built for grazing, this is the largest and most social species in its family; its northern subspecies lost its last known male, Sudan, in 2018 — which animal?
White rhinoceros: Species of large land mammal.
Tracing its formal origins to Aristotle and later shaped by Carl Linnaeus, this branch of biology studies the structure, classification and behavior of animals — which field?
The symbol for hassium is Hs. Hassium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Hs and atomic number 108.
The symbol for actinium is Ac. Actinium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ac and atomic number 89.

In what year was Kiefer Sutherland born?
Kiefer Sutherland: Kiefer William Frederick Dempsey George Rufus Sutherland (born 21 December 1966) is a British and Canadian actor.
In what year was Gene Hackman born?
Gene Hackman: Eugene Allen Hackman (January 30, 1930 – February 18, 2025) was an American actor.
In what year was Maggie Smith born?
Maggie Smith: Dame Margaret Natalie Smith (28 December 1934 – 27 September 2024) was a British actress.
In what year was Alexis Bledel born?
Alexis Bledel: Kimberly Alexis Bledel ( blə-DEL; born September 16, 1981) is an American actress and model.
In what year was Seth Rogen born?
Seth Rogen: Seth Aaron Rogen ( ROH-gən; born April 15, 1982) is a Canadian actor, comedian, filmmaker, and cannabis entrepreneur.
In what year was Emilia Clarke born?
Emilia Clarke: Clarke's television debut was a guest appearance in the BBC One medical soap opera Doctors in 2009, at age 22.
In what year was Brie Larson born?
Brie Larson: Brianne Sidonie Desaulniers (born October 1, 1989), known professionally as Brie Larson, is an American actress, singer and filmmaker.
In what year was Samantha Ruth Prabhu born?
Samantha Ruth Prabhu (born 28 April 1987) is an Indian actress who works predominantly in Telugu and Tamil films.
In what year was Dustin Hoffman born?
Dustin Hoffman: Dustin Lee Hoffman (born August 8, 1937) is an American actor and filmmaker.
In what year was Park Seo-joon born?
Park Seo-joon: Park Yong-kyu (Korean: 박용규; born December 16, 1988), better known by the stage name Park Seo-joon (박서준), is a South Korean actor.
In what year was Prince born?
Prince Rogers Nelson (June 7, 1958 – April 21, 2016), known mononymously as Prince, was an American singer, songwriter, musician, dancer, actor, and filmmaker.
In what year did Matthew Perry die?
Matthew Perry: Matthew Langford Perry (August 19, 1969 – October 28, 2023) was an American and Canadian actor.
In what year did Chadwick Boseman die?
Chadwick Boseman: Chadwick Aaron Boseman (November 29, 1976 – August 28, 2020) was an American actor and playwright.
In what year was The Pale Blue Eye first released?
The Pale Blue Eye is a 2022 American period mystery gothic thriller film written and directed by Scott Cooper, adapted from the 2006 novel by Louis Bayard.
In what year was The Woman King first released?
